posts.title: The Entourage Effect: Why THC % & Sativa/Indica isn’t important!
posts.body:
A higher THC percentage doesn’t automatically mean a better or even stronger experience.

Cannabis contains THC, CBD, other cannabinoids, and aromatic compounds called terpenes. The idea behind the entourage effect is that these compounds may interact and influence the overall experience rather than THC acting completely on its own.

Terpenes like limonene, myrcene, pinene, caryophyllene, and linalool contribute to a strain’s aroma and flavor and may also play a role in how the experience feels. Research into exactly how much terpenes alter cannabis effects is still developing, so the entourage effect shouldn’t be treated as completely proven science yet. (MDPI⁠￼)

Sativa, Indica & Hybrid Aren’t Very Reliable

The traditional Sativa, Indica, and Hybrid labels are commonly used to predict effectsSativa for energetic, Indica for relaxing, and Hybrid somewhere in between but real cannabis doesn’t fit neatly into those categories.

Research has found that Sativa and Indica labels do not reliably represent the actual genetics or full chemical profile of a strain. Two products both labeled “Indica” can have very different terpene and cannabinoid profiles and potentially produce very different experiences. (Nature⁠￼)

That’s why looking at the actual chemistry of the flower can be more useful than relying only on the name printed on the jar.

THC % Is Only One Number

THC percentage tells you how much THC is present it doesn’t tell you the entire experience.

A 20% THC strain with a terpene profile that works well for you may feel much more enjoyable than something testing at 30% THC. Dose, tolerance, cannabinoids, terpenes, consumption method, and your own body chemistry can all influence the experience.

How Strain Diary Handles It

Strain Diary goes beyond the traditional Sativa, Indica, and Hybrid labels.

When terpene information is available, Strain Diary uses the strain’s terpene and cannabinoid profile to create a more chemistry-based classification and show potential effects associated with that profile.

Instead of assuming every “Sativa” will feel energetic or every “Indica” will make you tired, the app helps you look at what is actually in the strain and learn which terpene profiles tend to work best for you.

The more strains you log, the easier it becomes to notice patterns between their chemistry and your personal experience.

Bottom line: Don’t choose cannabis based only on THC percentage or whether the package says Sativa, Indica, or Hybrid. Pay attention to the cannabinoids, terpenes, dose, and most importantly how different profiles actually affect you.

For educational purposes only. Not Medical Advice. Cannabis laws vary by location.

posts.title: Distillate: BDT vs. CDT 🌿
posts.body:
Distillate is a highly refined cannabis extract that contains mostly THC. The refining process removes many of the plant’s natural terpenes, so terpenes are often added back for flavor and aroma.

🍓 BDT — Botanically Derived Terpenes
BDTs come from non-cannabis plants and are commonly used to create stronger, fruitier, or candy-like flavors. They’re generally cheaper and are common in flavored carts and disposables.

🌿 CDT — Cannabis-Derived Terpenes
CDTs are extracted directly from cannabis. They tend to provide a more natural, strain-like flavor and aroma that resembles actual flower.

The Bottom Line:
🍬 BDT = Terpenes from other plants, often sweeter/flavored
🌱 CDT = Terpenes from cannabis, more flower-like

Neither automatically means a product is better or safer—quality, formulation, and proper testing matter too.

For educational purposes only.

posts.title: Live Rosin vs. Live Resin 🍯
posts.body:
Both live rosin and live resin are cannabis concentrates made using fresh-frozen flower to help preserve the plant’s cannabinoids and terpenes. The biggest difference is how they’re extracted.

🧊 Live Rosin
Live rosin is solventless. Fresh-frozen cannabis is typically made into hash, then pressed using heat and pressure to extract the concentrate. Because no chemical solvents are used, live rosin is often considered a more premium concentrate and usually costs more.

🧪 Live Resin
Live resin uses solvents, commonly hydrocarbons such as butane or propane, to extract cannabinoids and terpenes from fresh-frozen cannabis. The solvents are then removed during processing. Properly produced and tested live resin should meet limits for residual solvents.

The Bottom Line:
🌿 Live Rosin = Solventless, heat + pressure
🧪 Live Resin = Solvent-based extraction

Both can offer strong effects and flavorful, terpene-rich experiences the better choice mostly comes down to preference and product quality.

For educational purposes only. Effects can vary from person to person.

posts.title: THCA vs. Delta-9 THC  Whats the Differance?🌿
posts.body:
THCA is the natural precursor to Delta-9 THC. In fact, most cannabis flower even flower sold at licensed dispensaries contains much of its THC in the form of THCA before it’s heated.

🔥 When you smoke, vape, or dab flower, heat converts THCA into Delta-9 THC, the cannabinoid primarily responsible for the “high.”

THCA + Heat → Delta-9 THC

🌿 This means legitimate “THCA flower” isn’t a fundamentally different type of cannabis from typical dispensary flower. Both can be rich in THCA and become intoxicating when heated. The label “THCA flower” is often related to how the product is marketed, tested, or regulated rather than it being a completely different kind of weed.

Bottom line: Most weed is naturally high in THCA. What matters is the cannabinoid content, product quality, testing, and where it came from not simply whether the package says “THCA flower.”

For educational purposes only. Not Medical Advice. Cannabis laws vary by location.
